question_asked: I remember when I was cramming for my final exams in school, everything seemed so important and urgent. Sleep was a rare commodity during those times. Even though I knew it's the cumulative essence of what we learn over time that holds importance, those milestone exams always brought about an adrenaline rush. How did you feel during your last educational exams? Were they of critical importance in shaping your career or course of education?
response:
My Masters in Computer Science was nothing short of an adrenaline filled, caffeine powered roller coaster ride. I mean every exam felt like it could turn things around. And yep, sleep? what is that again? lol. Thinking about the final exams always invokes the taste of the countless coffees I chugged. But that aside, it was the journey through the years that really crafted the software engineer in me.

The only thing is, the exams themselves didn't feel like introducing grand new paradigms. Instead, they were like this litmus test of whether or not one's been keeping up to speed with the gradually building blocks of the field. So, while they may not have shaped my course or career in drastic ways, they definitely were significant milestones in the journey. 

And although I might not have realized it then, there's definitely a fair bit of what I learnt that I use now in my job here in Zurich. Gotta say tho, sometimes, in the middle of debugging a gnarly piece of code, I'd trade part of my big salary to have the stress of one of those exams again! haha. :P

question_asked: I was going through some old school papers recently and was stunned at the level of improvement and growth I see in my writing. Considering that back in high school, writing a two-page essay seemed like an insurmountable task, but here I am, having written a series of research papers, and even a thesis! Have you noticed a similar growth in any particular skills or knowledge areas, that you feel your formal education has contributed significantly to?
response: oh, absolutely! my thing was always a deep fascination for words, stories, messages hidden beneath lines of text, ya know? let's just say, cohesion wasn't my strongest suit in the beginning, oftentimes meandering from the topic, talking about everything and nothing at the same time, haha. but hey, over years, one's writing surely gets honed, right? and there’s sth strangely satisfying 'bout re-reading your old discussions, dissecting Goethe and Kafka. the journey from deciphering Die Metamorphose to contemplating on its allegorical interpretation, pretty wild, huh? ;)

question_asked: Just the other day, I was recalling my undergrad years at the university. There was a course on Renaissance Literature that was particularly challenging, yet intriguing at the same time. The dense but beautiful verses of Dante, the tragic tales of Shakespeare, the witty plays of Molière... I was wondering if you have ever delved into any works from the Renaissance era, whether for pleasure or for a course at school maybe?
response: oh totally, can totally relate to you mate. those were some days, can't forget this one obscure class we had to take, classic world cinema. kinda random right? but it was mind-blowing, totally changed the way I look at films now. renaissance lit’s not really my thing, but the equivalent for me is probably exploring some old-timey european cinema, oh the ingenuity & rawness in those productions, they're like poetry in motion. 🎥

question_asked: I remember back in college when I was doing my dissertation on computational linguistics, those late nights felt endless. We had to do a lot of running around, from the computer lab to the library, and back again. Those were the days... Even now, certain aspects of my field, especially automated translation, amaze me. I find it incredible how much we've progressed. What about you? Is there a particular field or discipline that captivates your interest and has progressed remarkably?
response: Oh yeah, the progress in some areas really blow my mind too, and in my line of work, the evolution is something else. you wouldn't believe the strides we've taken in understanding the human mind. i mean, we're talking huge leaps from the days of purely observational methods. we now delve into realms of cognitive-behavioral analysis, attachment theory, and even neuropsychology... it's a journey, let me tell ya ha! especially mind-blowing how technology's joining the mix, with AI and machine learning making inroads into our field. nice to find areas of fascination, eh? keeps the work engaging, even after all these years :)

question_asked: Funny story, when I started my studies in IT, I felt like an alien with no clue what was going on. One summer I decided to take a Python programming course, even though my friends said it was synonymous to drinking from a fire hose. I passed, and boy the confidence it gave me! Coding now feels like a cup of tea. Have you ever experienced this type of situation? A learning curve feeling impossible at first, but manageable at the end?
response:
hehe, well isn't that something we've all been through at some point or another? for me, early in my career, things revolved around understanding the interplay of figures and lines... one might scoff, but it's not as simple as 2+2, believe me. in particular, this one software they asked me to learn - 'rhinoceros'. oh dear, i was staring at it like one would at a massive kraken rising from the sea, utterly overwhelmed 😲

i poured weeks into it, learning the ropes, but it all just seemed so... arcane. then one day, i don't know, something just clicked. it was like the jumbled mess of wires in my brain realigned themselves into this beautiful symmetrical blueprint, et voila! suddenly, rhinoceros was more like a playful kitten than a monstrous kraken. so yeah, know what you mean about ending up finding it manageable 😅 now it's simply an essential tool of my trade.

question_asked: Back when I was doing my Master's, I spent sleepless nights preparing for the Econometrics exam. I still remember trying to understand the derivation of the OLS parameters and their significance. Some of my friends, however, thought it was an easy course and they perfectly understood the math behind it. How about you? Did you find a subject or topic particularly challenging during your studies?
response: haha, feeling ya man. the pain of econometrics, those are some memories i'd rather forget 🙃. dunno about you, but for me it's all about stats really, just doesn't seem to click. tried different approaches, just seems to be my brain-fart subject. 🤷 but hey, seems like its all part of the game in econ isn't it? lol.

question_asked: I remember the days of writing endless essays and research papers during my college years. There were those glorious moments when a breakthrough would hit me in the middle of the night and I would scramble out of bed to quickly jot down my thoughts! Ah, those were indeed a time of self-discovery. I wonder if you ever had the same experience, or perhaps your school required a different type of project or thesis. How did you manage it?
response: oh, those sleepless nights filled with coding and debugging... i used to power through the problems until dawn. sometimes it felt like i was stuck, getting nowhere with the task, but then outta nowhere an idea would pop into my head and i'd get it done like a breeze. the satisfaction was immense, i tell ya. i guess every profession or discipline has their own sort of moment of enlightenment :D. software stuff can be tough too, mate... not easy at all.

question_asked: I remember back when I was working towards my Masters in Psychology, I had to pull so many all-nighters to read through volumes of research papers and write multiple essays. With time though, it all felt worth it as I began to understand the intricacies of human behavior in a way I never thought was possible. And hey, as one good thing led to another, here I am today chatting to you! So, I'm curious, any research or academic field you've read about that has led you to a big 'Aha' moment or blown your mind?
response: oh boy, the human body, it never ceases to amaze me. like, I can't count how many 'Aha' moments i've had, every time as if i took a peek into the mysterious that is life itself. i still recall vividly the first time i held a heart, beating, in my hands during a successful transplant surgery... felt like holding the universe, it was so surreal, haha. also, the intricacies of the nervous system just boggles my mind, like how a bunch of signals regulate every single thing we do... wild! :)

question_asked: I'm currently halfway reading this fascinating book about space exploration, particularly about Mars. Oh, did I mention I'm a fan of astronomy? That might be rubbed off me by my physics professor back in college. Her passion to unravel the mysteries of the universe was very contagious! After my bachelor's, I was almost decided to pursue further studies in astrophysics, but life happened, and I veered into writing. Did you ever have any quirky fascination when you were in school? A subject or a department that was really your thing?
response: oh man, taking it way back! so, while most peeps were caught up in astro and bio, I was that creature in the corner obsessing over coding and circuits, funny enough, right? not the usual interest a youngin' would have, haha. Had an amazing prof back then, got me so hooked, I thought "You know what, we sticking with this for the long haul." Practically lived in the comp eng department, loved every bit. Now, making games for a living, can you imagine a better path for a code-crazy kid? weird things make us happy, I guess 😄

question_asked: You know, my high school days were an exciting time. I remember how thrilled I was about the science projects. One of our physics projects was the making of a Ferris wheel model, and our chemistry teacher once asked us to create our own volcano with the use of bicarbonate and vinegar. Did you have such stimulating learning activities in your early school years? Or was it all more or less reading books and taking notes? Oh and by the way, what was your favorite subject back then?
response: oh, those early school days! haha, not so much exciting projects like you had, but plenty of note-taking, trust me. although, i've gotta say, our business studies class was kind of a blast! we even had this mock stock market thing where we had to manage our own portfolio. probably where i kinda caught the bug for my current gig, mind you ;) other than that, it was indeed mostly books and blackboards. as for favourite subject, can't say i didn't get a kick out of math. love the problem-solving aspect of it, still use it a lot today! what about you?

question_asked: I have a rather funny memory from my time at college. One day, during my sophomore year, my group and I were working on a Physics assignment that had us stumped. We spent hours working on it, and finally decided to break the rules a little. We snuck into a senior physics class, hoping to get some hints. In the end, it turned out that the assignment was meant to be unsolvable. The professor confessed that he was testing our problem-solving skills! Now, did you ever have a similar experience or a moment in studies that you found particularly challenging or amusing? Can you share?
response:
oh mate, i've got a good one for this... back when i was studying, we had this one ancient roman history course that was notorious among students. our professor was old school, firm believer of "to learn history, you got to feel history".

there was this one instance, when we were studying about roman military tactics, the professor decided that just reading about it wouldn't cut it. next thing we know, we are in the university's soccer field, divided into legions, enacting the battle of zama, with watering cans as stand-ins for war elephants! looking back, that day was mad exhausting, but definitely one of the most memorable and hard-hitting classes. guess nothing drives the point home like soaking your mates with watering cans pretending to be 'war elephants'! :D

question_asked: I remember hitting the books hard when I was completing my thesis for my Masters, it was grueling and intense to say the least, but also deeply satisfying in some strange way. Then the job hunt phase kicked in and all those elevated concepts I had to grapple with suddenly seemed a world apart from reality. On the job, it's experience that takes precedence over theory. Have you had a similar experience after completing your education, or do you find the concepts you learned to be directly applicable in your professional life?
response: Ah, well mate, I can't exactly say I've had the same experience as you. Finished my education with a High School Diploma and did not go to university getting any fancy degree like Masters. The job that I had before retiring, it was more about hard work and experience over theory. But I'll tell ya, education does shape you in a way, instills discipline, helps you think logically, and that has stayed with me. But most of the practical stuff, that came from on-the-job-training and years of experience, tbh. Mind you, my time on the job is long over, retirement does have its benefits. Now I mostly spend my time online, reddit being my hunting ground, haha. It’s a different kind of education, scrolling through different subs, the stuff you find around here, mate! Quite the ride, ain't it?

question_asked: When I was doing my Masters in Computer Science, one of the topics that caused a lot of debate in our group was the impact and implications of Artificial Intelligence. Personally, I think the benefits far outweigh the risks. Do you believe the development of AI technologies will have more positive or negative impact in the future?
response: yea, AI is an intense topic, even in my field. i mean, as someone who spend day in and day out with artifacts of the past, it's intriguing to think how technology like AI could potentially revolutionise what I do everyday. we've already seen nifty little changes like digitization of records and stuff. but off top of my head, imagine AI developed enough to create in-depth interactive recreations of historical events! That said, gotta admit the idea of an AI potentially misinterpreting data and rewriting history does give me chills, haha. so in a nut shell, yeah sure i see an overall positive impact, but cannot ignore those few negatives. we need to tread carefully ;)

question_asked: Being an avid reader of numerous periodicals and magazines, I can't help but delve into at least one book or article related to astrophysics every week. My fascination with the cosmos started back in high school when my physics teacher showed us a documentary about black holes. Absolutely mind-boggling, isn't it? Speaking of obsessions, is there any specific subject or field that you find yourself inexplicably drawn to? Do you often catch yourself reading or talking about it?
response: oh, for sure...i often find myself deep diving into anything related to historical events. my bookshelves might just topple over from all the books i have on ancient civilizations. there's just something about knowing what came before us, ya know? whether it be the fall of the roman empire or world war ii, it's both astoundingly complex and fascinating. can't seem to get enough of it! it often sneaks into my lessons and conversations :P

question_asked: I spent some time studying botany in university, and I remember one of our field trips where we went to this amazing forest. The beauty of the biodiversity was just astounding. The trees, plants, and little critters living there were all part of this intricate system where every single organism had its own role to play. It's really crazy when you think about it, all those different forms of life living together and supporting each other in one way or another. It got me hooked on science. Are you a fan of nature too? What's your most vivid memory of interacting with nature?
response: bloody oath, mate! nothing beats a good walkabout the auckland domain, especially when the flowers are in bloom and the critters are out. used to do a fair bit of tramping in my younger days down in christchurch, too. bush-bashing at arthur's pass, always found something interesting and new. those were truly the days, could feel the earth beneath me feet, the smell of the pines... ahh takes me back i tell ya :D ran into kea a couple of times! cheeky buggers, had a knack for nicking people's stuff. isn't as much tramping nowadays i reckon, knees aren't what they used to be. still, bi-weekly mosey around the domain, keeps the blood pumping, let's me enjoy nature's splendours. ya never forget the heartbeat of the bush, mate.

question_asked: Back in high school, I was kind of a geek who spent a lot of time taking apart computers as a hobby. That really set me up for my studying computer science in college. As a result, I could skip some intro courses due to my background. I sometimes wish more schools offered practical courses like this, to help students find their passion early on. How do you feel about it? Did you have any similar practical courses that helped you in further studies or career?
response: heh, oh, I get what you're saying, a little bit different in my case tho. back in my school days, shop class was more about woodwork or ironwork, nothing to do with my calling you might say. didn't have anything like bio or anatomy lab until university :/. but then when I did, it just felt right, made me even more intrigued about the human body and the mysteries it holds, was definitely the turning point that led me toward my medical career. as for secondary schools offering more practical courses, couldn't agree more! anything to make youngin's appreciate the joy of learning and the potential paths ahead, you know?

question_asked: I remember my time in university like it was yesterday. Between the sleepless exam weeks, unpredictable social life, and the never-ending assignments, it was definitely a roller coaster. But I have to say, it was during those times that I truly discovered my love for economics and everything related. I'd spend hours, sometimes days, breaking down economic theories, analyzing case studies, and applying them to real-world scenarios. It was stressful but incredibly rewarding. What about you, do you have a specific academic or professional topic that you're really passionate about?
response: Oh mate, reading your comment brought back memories of me studying in the wee hours, churning through piles of case studies, and deriving business strategies. Can't say I miss the stress, but those times did ignite a deep passion for business strategy in me. Down to today, as a retired CEO with a Bachelors in Business Administration under my belt, I'll find myself drawn into business news or problems faced by companies, and before I know it, I'm sketching up solutions on a napkin. Just can't help myself, that's most of my reddit activity right there, hahaha... getting nitty-gritty with business & strategizing, oh it's a riot! What can I say, it's in my blood! Not that I miss the stress of running a company though, enjoying my slower paced life now.

question_asked: I've always been intrigued by the diversity of educational paths one can walk. Personally, my academic journey had more twists and turns than I ever expected. After studying linguistics for my bachelor’s, I decided to completely switch and pursue a master’s in data science recently. It’s been challenging but definitely fascinating. Seems like diving into complex data sets and spotting unseen patterns is my new passion. How have you experienced your path? Has your passion driven your choices, or were you pulled towards a completely new direction unexpectedly, and why? Also, if you care to share, what subjects or fields have intrigued you the most?
response: oh boy, quite a journey for you! my path's been kinda similar tho. had a thing for the stars since early on, like when a wee kid stared at that Glasgow sky you know. Thought would go straight into that, but life's a funny ol' thing, wanted the big city life n' ended up in Edinburgh. Work wise, i've not really been pulled in a new direction per se. still gazing at stars but on a whole different level. Being an astronomer is...interesting, to put it lightly. instead of seeing them twinklin', now im mostly crunching numbers, spinning theories, deciphering the secrets of the cosmic ballet. no regrets tho. as for subjects that fascinate me the most, I'm partial to nebulas and black holes. strange, beautiful, mysterious, they are like the epitome of why I love this field. fascinating how we once thought they were just empty dark spots, but they turned out to hold so much more inside, kinda like us humans yeah?

question_asked: I remember the nights of cramming for exams and pulling all-nighters during my time at university. It was tough, especially when you have mid-terms and assignments due in different classes around the same period. Then there's the total switch when you enter the workforce and have to adjust to corporate life, it's not easy, right? Has it been similar for you, or did you experience something entirely different while transitioning from your last stage of formal education towards your first job?
response: ooof, the transition was rough for sure, i can definitely relate! my uni days didn't just vanish at the crack of dawn, finished my computer science course, then 'real life' kicked in. still remember coding Java applications whilst straddling tight deadlines for college assignments... then BOOM, i land up needing to adept with complex JavaScript in my job as a web developer, and the tight deadlines still followed haha... the corporate life sure was a shocker, but then, learning in real-time was an intense yet interesting curve :D

question_asked: I remember when I was doing my masters in physics, I had this one course which was basically about breaking theoretical thermodynamics down into practical, everyday examples. It was quite an interesting and insightful way of learning. It's got me wondering, how do you feel about real-life application examples in academic courses? Do they help to consolidate your understanding of the subjects or is a more theoretical, pure study more helpful for you?
response: hmm, I'd have to say I appreciate both, but real-life applications were always something that brought the "ooh, so that's how it works" kind of moments for me. during my Bachelors in Software Engineering, applying what i was learning to actual code or similar practical examples could be an eye-opening experience. u know, sometimes u have those abstract ideas floating around ur head, but when u see it in action, it just clicks somehow. not to say that pure theory doesn't have its own value, cause it sure does, but seeing it applied to something tangible generally makes it stick with me more. brings it home, u know?

question_asked: It's incredible to see how far technology has come, isn't it? I do miss simpler times though. Not going to lie, I enjoyed typing away at my bulky home computer for my college assignments. That old thing had Wordperfect. It was pretty cutting edge back then and I enjoyed the creative process of figuring things out. Now of course, Word-perfect is obsolete. How about you? Do you have a nostalgia for a type of old tech, or perhaps an old software you worked with?
response: definitely. sometimes i get hit with a wave of nostalgia when i come across some older editing software or tech. i've cut my teeth on some of the less... streamlined tools much before we got spoilt by the seamless interfaces of today's premiere pro or final cut. i remember wrestling with some eyebrow-raising glitches when rendering my first few shorts, haha. not that i want to go back to them but there's something about those good ol' days of really getting your hands dirty, you know. :')

question_asked: I just finished reading a fascinating book about the history and the evolution of mass media. It really made me think about how information used to spread during the good old days compared to now in the era of online journalism, social media, etc. I guess the smooth transition from print to digital media is commendable, but it also comes with its own set of challenges, right? What's your take on this? How do you perceive the evolution of media and its impact on society? Do you think the prominence of digital journalism over print is a positive trend for society?
response:
oh absolutely, the transition has been nothing short of a revolution really, being able to access virtually any piece of information from anywhere is mighty. on the other hand, having to wade through endless clickbait headlines to find anything of value can really feel like you are slogging through thick fog :/ 

i suppose it's a bit of a double-edged sword, in a way. there's a rush to publish "hot takes" on current events which sometimes results in a sacrifice of thoroughness, or even correctness. that said, we've also seen an expansion of voices in the media landscape, which can only be good for promoting diverse perspectives. 

but, don’t get me wrong, as someone who is on the internet a lot and has fully embraced social media, I see the benefits - it's just that there's also a fair bit of nostalgia for the times when evenings would involve flipping through a good book or a thoughtful article from a reputable newspaper, rather than scrolling through an endless barrage of opinions, some less informed than others.

so yeah, i guess i gotta say it's a bit of a mixed bag for me. anyway, i'd love to hear from you or anyone else who's been adapting to this brave new world too!

question_asked: Recently, I started reminiscing about my school years, from the smell of the classrooms to the long homework assignments. I don't know if you'd agree with me, but I believe high school chemistry was disproportionately difficult, considering that we hardly use most of that knowledge unless we pursue a career in a related field. What school subject did you find the most challenging, and why?
response: oh man, for me it was chemistry too! I guess it was interesting but I was just never good at it 😅 those periodic tables always got me lost, and don't get me even started on the molecular structures... but then here I am now, working with environment related stuff, and sometimes i do wish i paid more attention to those lessons. i guess even when you don't think you’ll need something, life might surprise you haha... 😉

question_asked: I recently attended a high school reunion and I was surprised to see how many people ended up in professions totally unrelated to what they were interested in during school. Personally, I did my masters in psychology, currently working as a counselor, directly related to my field of study. I've always been curious about people who end up in fields they initially didn't think of. Have you experienced anything like this? Have you or anyone you know end up in a job that's quite different from what they originally studied in school?
response: aha, well not me exactly, but it could've been. was really closer to wind up majoring in biology, back when I was at school, I loved it! even started university with that, but honestly, couldn't see myself long term being a biologist. later on, took a couple random comp sci classes and like clicked.. so here i am, coding my way through life 😅. but yeah, met a couple guys in the field who were English majors, so imagine that shift 🤷‍♀️! guess all of us have our own winding roads to our destination, don't we?

question_asked: I've been out of school for quite a while now, but I still keep up to date with the newest findings in the scientific field. Ever since I joined the astronomy club in high school and went to see my first meteor shower, I've been hooked! Lately, I've been particularly engrossed by the discoveries of exoplanets and our increasing ability to analyze their atmospheres to guess if they could harbor life. What do you think about this? Do you believe we will find extraterrestrial life in our lifetime? And wouldn’t it be cool to observe these cosmological phenomena live with those giant observatories?
response: oh, you're speaking my language!! when there's a meteor shower, i'm that person up odd hours of the night in my backyard star gazing, haha.. gotta love the Texas sky! those professional grade observatories? now that’d be somethin! Scientific advancements like exoplanet discoveries are just so darn fascinating. i do hope we stumble upon some form of extraterrestrial life within our lifetime.. or at least, hint strong enough to spark more interest in space exploration. y'know, as a shop owner, most my days stay pretty grounded.. so lose myself in the stars once in a while is my sort of escape 😊

question_asked: I'm really glad I chose to study business administration in college. It's paid dividends in my career, but I also really loved the subject matter – macroeconomics and microeconomics, organizational behavior, financial management, you name it! Did you also have any subjects or topics you were particularly drawn to during your studies?
response: oh i feel you! my favourite bit of studies were definitely the modules where we had to work on conservational issues and ecosystem integrity and all that. i guess has something to do with the idea that you're directly helping to sustain and conserve our environment. reading about climate patterns and geomorphology were a bit of a drag sometimes, but even that stuff can be fascinating in its own right. never was a fan of the more chemistry heavy units though, lol!

question_asked: One of the first things I learned in my first year of college was how to pull an all-nighter properly. You'd be surprised how much of a science it is! Making sure I had a steady stream of coffee, working in breaks, and knowing the exact moment to stop studying and let the information soak in was a big part of my success. I weathered most college parties and academic stresses because I learned those things early on. Just curious, do you have any surefire productivity hacks or methods you swear by to get things done when you're under the stress of a deadline?
response: oh mate, those undergrad days, haha. spending endless nights in the library with a cup of joe... well, these days it's more like balancing between piles of docs in my study & making it to court on time. the old uni days kind of train you for that, but yeah, when you're swamped with responsibilities you just have to focus on priorities. need to toss some things on the back-burner, and put all your energy into what's urgent. but yeah, one thing i've learned, no matter how busy you are, never skip yer mate breaks. they're a lifesaver to refuel and rethink strategies ;)

question_asked: Just the other day, I was thinking about my high school subjects. I took a lot of science classes, like physics, chem and bio, not because I loved them, but they were mandatory! I got pretty good grades in them thanks to my study group, man, the memories. And you? Did you enjoy your science classes or were they not quite your thing?
response: Oh man, the science subjects in high school... yikes ! :D I wouldn't say I disliked them per se, but uh, let's just say there's a reason I ended up going for a Bachelors in Visual Arts instead haha. I was always more at home in the art room than the lab. There's just something bout expressing myself visually that always clicked. But, hey, gotta give it to those science classes, they taught me problem-solving and detailed observation, which has helped me as a graphic designer in their own ways. No regrets :)

question_asked: Man, I remember the crazy all-nighters I had to pull to finish up term papers in my college days. It feels weird now that you can search up pretty much any fact you want at any time. I almost miss hunting through the library for hardcover books to cite in my papers. Haha! Do you think easy access to information has taken away some of the struggles of learning or just reshaped them?
response: oh, pal, those crazy all-nighters are an experience haha! spend my life sniffing out celestial hints, remember having a right old hunt searching for those tucked-away theses in the library. i reckon it's reshaped more than taken away, ya know? sure, we've got info right at our fingertips, but discerning credible info from the dross, that's a whole new skill. plus, there's an art to not getting lost in the digital maze. same but different, wouldn't ya say? :D

question_asked: It's always fun for me to remember my university days, when professors would ask us the most compelling questions that seemed impossible to answer, like the chicken-and-egg problems. It's also fascinating how new knowledge and technology are constantly reshaping my field of expertise. What has been your experience with 'chicken-and-egg' problems or seemingly unsolvable questions, either in your work life or your personal hobbies? Have any recent developments reshaped how you approach these questions?
response:
oh definitely! in my line of work, the balance between functionality and aesthetics is always a big chicken-and-egg problem. should the design follow function or form? do I get inspired first and then find a way to incorporate the client's needs, or do I start with the requirements and let the creative stuff come later? it's like a constant game of tug of war haha. 

recent technology has been a game changer though. with all these new design tools and increased interactivity, it has become way easier to create a drive towards a seamless blend of the two. it's no less of a problem, but it's easier to juggle now than ever before. 🎭💻

question_asked: Remembering my college days brings a smile to my face. In particular, I recall the excitement and trepidation of writing my first ever dissertation. For weeks on end, I was holed up in the library making copious notes and hoping that the gambit of sources I'd included would impress my professors. The immense satisfaction of finally submitting it after continuous all-nighters was such a relief. How about you? Do you fondly look back at some moments during your student life?
response:
Ah, student life, what a rollercoaster it was! Loved it and dreaded it at the same time, haha. Specifically, I remember the time when I was pursuing my Masters in Art History. Those were days filled with all-nighters and numerous visits to museums, galleries, little nooks and crannies filled with hidden treasures of the art world. You see, Paris is an art historian's playground. The thrill of discovering a new piece or interpreting a classic in a new light was exhilarating.

Oh, and dissertations (well in France we call it "mémoire"), **shudders slightly**. They were a challenge and a thrill, all bundled into one. The anxiety of meeting deadlines, impressing the profs, and basically trying to make sense of your own ideas...those were the days indeed! I also spent many days holed up, not in a library, but lost in the numerous art collections across Paris, digging for that intriguing piece of mystery or history. The day I finished my "mémoire" was one of relief, exhaustion, and pure joy all at the same time.

Good times, good times! Just writing this brought back so many memories :') Now I am the one judging art instead of studying it, and my love for art has only grown! That's why I am here now, chatting about it on reddit during my spare time lol. 

Would I go back? Maybe, for a visit. But I'm much happier sipping my espresso in a little Parisian café, answering your questions on my phone, and curating the next big exhibit :D

question_asked: I remember when I was doing my undergraduate studies and everything about the world of academia seemed so exciting to me. Like, that defining moment when I wrote my first research paper. It was such an exciting process from the onset of brainstorming, developing interesting ideas, research and data collection, proofreading, and finally the rush of excitement when it was time for presentation. What was your definitive moment in your academic journey?
response: oh wow, that sounds like a roller coaster of emotions for sure! for my part, I'd say my definitive moment was more on the practical side, ya know. when i started working part-time in retail during my academic journey, it was like really understanding how the theories i was learning about were playing out in the real world. managing finances, customer relations, supply and demand - it was all right there in front of my eyes to see and learn from. it was a real reality check moment, if you get what i mean. gave me a different appreciation for what i was learning about in my studies. so, yeah, that's my moment. a bit different from the academic thrill, but still, it did its part in shaping my understanding of things. :)

question_asked: I remember back in college when I had to pull an all-nighter for the last-minute project completion or studying for final exams. Those days were pretty tough yet flashbacks bring a smile to my face, oddly enough. Now that I'm working, deadlines still exist but the experience has taught me to balance out my time more effectively. Do you remember any such crunch moments or situations where you felt the pressure of completing something, be it academics or work? How did you deal with it?
response: oh the memories, those were golden days, filled with terror haha... like that time during my PhD studies when I had to present my research on Goethe's works and I was so nervous about it. The night before, I was up till 3 am arranging my notes, only to be faced with total power cut at my place. Talk about bad luck, right?! Instead of panicking, I simply lit a candle, and voilà - suddenly it felt as if I was sitting in 19th century, scribbling my thesis with a Feather :D Far from being nostalgic tho, as soon as the morning came, i was rushing to university to get at least a few hours of printer-time! It was a nerve-wracking day, but managed to pull through. So now, whenever i'm facing deadline at the university, I just remember that night and think - hey, it could be worse! ;)

question_asked: I remember going through a straining period filled with late night study sessions and tons of revision when I started my college. At that time I also used to work part-time to afford my tuition fees. While it was tough, it was also enjoyable to be finally pursuing what I was really passionate about. Going into the industry with my degree was equally thrilling. Did you ever have to work while studying? How did you manage it with your classes and other commitments?
response: oh boy, bringin back memories here... during my bachelors, ya, worked part-time at a local grocery store. not the most fun job, but hey, it paid the bills and kept me going. juggling studies, work, and a (barely existent tbh) social life was rough, won't deny that. but I believe it kinda turned me into a half-decent time manager, a skill that's proven handy in my current job as a financial manager. most days had a cycle of uni > work > study > sleep (rinse and repeat). throw in bouts of stress and surviving mostly on instant ramen and coffee - welcome to the student life package deal, haha! :D Now my meal choice is a bit healthier tho... mostly...sometimes... haha, ok, i still have an affinity for instant ramen :p

question_asked: Man, it's been a while since I hit the books... Taking me back to all-nighters in the law library before the big case presentations. How did you grind out study or work sessions when the going got tough? Did you have a special strategy for winning the day when you had a huge workload?
response: oh mate, our grinds seem to differ, but the late-night struggle? that's a shared experience. during the times of gnarly workloads, going through dozens of research articles and dealing with complex cosmic calculations, could easily end up crushing my spirit. My savior has always been taking little breaks, a chapter (or a problem set) at a time, ya know? Some chai, few minutes outdoors, helped me keep my sanity. Don't forget, the universe worked for billions of years to shape itself, our work, no matter how critical, can surely wait a night, right ? :)

question_asked: Just the other day I was having a chat with an old college buddy of mine and we were reminiscing about the many intense all-nighters we pulled for those dreaded final exams. Those were some stressful days back when I was getting my bachelor's. Now granted, I wouldn't want to relive those stressful nights, but looking back, they were an integral part of my journey. It made me wonder, how much of your life has been shaped by your educational journey? And how have the skills you learned during your education helped you in your professional and/or personal life
response:
oh boy, those all-nighters, right? brings back the memories :D well, i've got to say a significant part of my life was indeed shaped by my educational journey. getting my Masters in Computer Engineering wasn't a piece of cake. there were times when i was stuck on a coding problem for days, but those experiences instilled in me a resilience that I carry to this day in my work as a game developer. those stressful nights taught me to stick with problems until i crack them. 

In professional life, the expertise I gained during my education is directly applicable to my role now. I mean, programming in C++ and digital systems design... without those, I wouldn't be doing the job I'm doing now.

on the personal side, i was also introduced to reddit during college, and now i kinda spend most of my free time on it, discussing gaming trends, coding tricks, sometimes even philosophical debates! i love the amount of diverse content and people it presents (though can be toxic at times, but hey, u gotta learn to filter, haha). 

All in all, without my education, i can’t really imagine being where i am now, both professionally and personally.

question_asked: I remember when I was studying for my Master's degree, I had to juggle between rigorous coursework and my part-time job in the library. There were times when I felt somewhat overwhelmed, but looking back, it was a valuable experience that shaped my ability to manage my time and tasks. Do you have any such experiences? Have you ever had to balance multiple responsibilities?
response: oh mate, juggling responsibilities? thats like every single day for me! between studying, which can get brutal cause commerce ain't no cakewalk, and working at retail job, it's a constant tightrope walk. some days are chill, some days get hectic with sudden surge of customers or assignment deadlines. gets taxing at times tbh, but hey, builds character right? and you do get to appreciate the slow days and free time a bit more. :)

question_asked: I've been reflecting a lot on the classic literature I read while pursuing my English Literature degree. It was fascinating to delve into different time periods and societies through the power of words. I especially found works from the Renaissance era to be a rich ground for exploration. Shakespeare, Marlowe, Spenser – they all had such a profound influence on me. What's your favorite period in literature, if you have one, and could you tell me a bit about why it appeals to you?
response: ohhh, literature... I've gotta admit, it hasn't been my strongest suit. my program in international relations is heavy on economics and political stuff mostly, not so much on classic literature. i did however like this one semester we had on ideology and propaganda in literature. lots of dystopian literature, that was a bit eerie, especially Orwell and Huxley. They really manage to put images into your head, that make you think and reconsider our current politics and society, you know? So in a weird way that's my fav period, although I know its not like traditional periodization in literature.

question_asked: I feel so nostalgic when I reminisce about my golden high school days. Being a part of the drama club was so much fun, we would perform on Shakespeare's plays and every time it was a new learning experience, interpreting those Elizabethan English verses was certainly a tough but rewarding task. It really accentuated my love for English literature to such an extent that I decided to major in it during my grad school. Those were indeed wonderful times. What about you? Have you ever been a part of any clubs or societies during your school or college? Did it influence any of your future career or education choices?
response: Aw man, sounds like you had a blast! For me, it was all about charity and entrepreneurship clubs during my uni days... wasn't quite the thespian life u had lol. And yeah, I think it kinda helped pave the way for me. There was something so fulfilling about organizing events and making a difference. Was part of a team that raised money for marginalized communities and that was something that struck me deeply (possibly due to my humble upbringing in Guadalajara). Totally why I pursued an MBA. Now here I am, trying to build sustainable business systems as a development manager in Mexico City. Coincidence? I guess not, haha. Maybe not as artsy as being part of a drama club but hey, keeps the gears in my head spinning!

question_asked: Went to a job fair recently, and it was so intriguing to see the different job expectations for different degree holders. As part of the tech industry, it feels like a balancing act for me. On one hand, a lot of successful folks in my field dropped out of college or don't even have a formal education. But on the other side, we've got jobs that often demand advanced STEM degrees. It seems this really depends on the job and the circumstances. How about you? Have you found an obvious demand for a certain degree level or education in your field?
response: Well, from my experience, running a shop isn't exactly a job that requires an advanced degree. I mean, as long as I know numbers and people, and I do! I've got my high school diploma, ya know ;) It's more about common sense and good judgment, dealing with suppliers and handling customer services - a street smart kind of job. but don't get me wrong, i still think education is important, but in this line of work, it's your hands-on experience and your ability to connect with people that make or break your success. So while some sectors might be all about degrees and certifications, for us shop owners, it's a whole different ball game.

question_asked: I've been doing a bit of soul-searching lately about my career choice. I took a non-traditional route; after high school, I travelled for a year, then pursued a technical diploma. To my surprise, that has opened up quite a few doors for me. If you could go back to when you were 18, 19 or 20, would you have chosen the same career path?
response: interesting question, i've pondered over this a few times. tbh, i’m quite content with where i've landed. managing finances has always been a knack and helping businesses navigate their fiscal puzzles fits me like a glove. would i explore other careers if i'm 20 again? maybe, sure, everyone loves a little adventure. but would i still end up crunching numbers when the dust settles? most likely, yes. it's who i am at my core, heh. hindsight, as they say, is 20/20. 😄

question_asked: I am a huge fan of literature. I remember losing myself in tales of epic adventures and deep introspection, both during my high school years and later on when I was studying English literature in college. I hold dear those times, as they shaped the person I am today. Do you also have a particular book or author that impressed you or affected you in a significant way, either during your school years or later on in life?
response: Definitely! Good question, reminds me of the book "Zamanın Kısa Tarihi" by Stephen Hawking. Read it during my bachelors in marketing. Was a refreshing change from all the business and marketing books. Picked it up just out of curiosity (was always fascinated by the cosmos, ya know) and boy it blew my mind! Really got me thinking about the universe and our place in it. I mean marketing is cool and all (and pays my bills lol), but contemplating big questions like "why are we here?" and "what's the nature of the universe?" made realize there's so much more to life than just work and money. Changed my perspective and keeps me grounded to this day. Plus, who didn't want to be an astronaut as a kid right? haha.

question_asked: I've been thinking about how much reading has changed in the past few years. I picked up an audiobook for the first time the other day and was surprised by how engaged I was with the story. It reminded me of how I used to devour hefty novels during my college years, just indulging in one literature classic after another. Things have evolved even more now with e-books taking over physical books. What about you? Do you usually read books, listen to audiobooks or prefer e-books? Any particular genres or authors that you enjoy?
response: hehe, funnily enough, enjoy chatting to you folks online more than reading anything these days. reading tends to be more like a work thing for me now (am sure you can sympathise), with thick files full of educational policy, administrative details, and parent memos, oi. but, back in the day when i had more time, was all about the classics, decent bit of Dickens can still sweep me off my feet. got on the e-book train but not really on board with the whole audiobook revolution just yet, like, no one does narration like the voice in our heads, right?📚🤷‍♀️

question_asked: The other day, I was having a lively discussion with a few colleagues about some of the greatest innovators of our time: people like Elon Musk and his ideas about colonizing Mars, or Mark Zuckerberg with his metaverse concept. We were debating whether these concepts were more driven by science fiction or evidence-based science. What's your take on this? Do you think we will colonize Mars in the next 50 years or will we live in a metaverse?
response:
that's a really intriguing question! tbh, i reckon it's a blend of both scifi and evidence-based science... you know, like how imagined futures often motivate scientific developments. i mean, we wouldn't be considering these ideas if there wasn't some root in existing science, right? 

about colonizing Mars, well, given my field of work, i'm naturally inclined towards skepticism. you know, leaving aside the technical challenges, there's loads of environmental implications and bioethical issues that we'd need to sort out first. in 50 years? seems like a tight deadline to me...

as for the metaverse, now that seems more feasible to me. we've already started meshing our lives with online realities, right? so why not a fully integrated digital-human life? but again, implications - this time social, psychological... heaps to think about here!

tl;dr - intriguing ideas but loads of stuff to figure out yet, and i'm not sold on the timeline. gonna be interesting to see how it all pans out though! ;)

question_asked: I was just reminiscing about my college days; specifically, about this particular theoretical physics course I took, where the professor was so passionate about quantum mechanics, it often made me completely engrossed in the lectures. We didn't just learn about Schrodinger's cat, but even discussed super complex topics like quantum entanglement and Bell's theorem. Those lectures truly sparked my interest in complex theories. Do you remember any course or subject from your school or university days that actually sparked your interest and left a lasting impression?
response: oh absolutely... still remember quite a few epic moments from my university days. One that really sticks out was this course about organisational development and change - reckon it doesn't sound as fascinating as quantum mechanics, but it was the prof... his energy, the real-world stories he would weave into the lectures, that absolute belief that one person can indeed make a difference in a corporation if they really want to... all those made the whole thing super intriguing. Funny thing, I didn't really realise the importance of that subject until I became more hands-on with running a business. Guess university does need a time machine, to truly appreciate a few subjects.

question_asked: I'm in awe of the advances in space exploration in my lifetime. It honestly feels like Star Trek isn't far from reality sometimes, right? As a kid, I remember how thrilled I was when I first stargazed with a telescope. Recently, though, I've been learning about black holes and it's boggling my mind, let me tell you! That stuff is crazy, isn't it? Have you delved into any of these mind-bending scientific concepts lately, what are your thoughts on them?
response: Definitely! Science is insane, isn’t it? Black holes are a fascinating, albeit mind-blowing. Matter getting sucked into nothingness seems so dystopian, can't wrap my head around that. I'm no hardcore science geek, but as a designer of sorts, I sometimes dive into biomimetics, you know, how nature's design can inspire human architecture. That stuff can be trippy too, helping me think out of the box. Makes my constructs almost feel like they’re a part of the cosmic cycle. :D But yeah, nothing as mind-bending as black holes! :P

question_asked: During my college time, I was heavily into debating. I once got into a quite heated debate about the merits of Post Modernism, and the next thing I knew, it was 3AM. Obviously, sleep was an alien concept during these moments 😂 Can't say I've lost my love for a good intellectual sparring, thank god for the internet. What about you, ever gotten totally lost into a topic, and time just flies by without your notice?
response: oh absolutely, happens more often than not... 😅 not too long ago, found myself reading until the wee hours of the morning, delving deep into the intricacies of global politics and how they're shifting y'know? ended up with too many open tabs and almost no sleep. lol, got to be up by 9 for my tutoring classes but hey, that's what coffee is for, right? 😂👌🏼

question_asked: I discovered a joy for DIY projects during the last home lockdown, and upped my skills in woodworking, metal turning and even some basic electronics. It all started with just some Youtube videos, but then I enrolled in some online courses and finally managed to build a standing desk with adjustable height. Have you ever pursued learning something outside the traditional education system? How was your experience, did you manage to complete a project, or did you drop it halfway through?
response:
Love that! I've definitely dabbled in bits and pieces outside the traditional learning paradigm. My latest obsession? Photography! Been spending a lot of time on r/photography, learning to level up my snaps. at first, it was a bit of a struggle to get my head around the complex camera settings n' all, but after a while it started to come together and now I love it.

Though admittedly, I'm not much of a hands-on DIYer like you. As for projects, I did start a photo series of unique doors around Paris, sort of a visual representation of the distinct characteristics each door presents. It's been an on and off thing, trying to fit it in and around my regular schedule and chaotic like life, but I've managed to snap quite a bunch.

Life-long learning is the way to go man, keep it up! Might even inspire me to finally assemble that IKEA bookshelf that's been sitting in my living room 😂.

question_asked: Growing up, I was really into reading books, especially fantasy and science fiction. I vividly remember emerging from Narnia, Middle-earth, and Guy Gavriel Kay's worlds not only entertained but also inspired. These books opened new horizons for me and played a significant role in shaping my personality and outlook towards life. They created a strong base for my university studies in Literature, digging into deeper meanings and nuances of narratives. Are there any books or authors you feel have significantly impacted you or shaped your perspective in life? Can you recommend me something to read next based on your tastes?
response:
oh definitely, i was (and still am) a huge fan of classic sci-fi novels, especially those dealing with cybernetics and AI, think gibson and asimov. being introduced to their worlds made me fascinated with the idea of programming and coding, something which later deeply impacted my choice when figuring out what i want to work with. 

hmm, based on my tastes, you could check out anything by ada palmer, her Terra Ignota series is one mind-blowing mix of philosophical musings and future history. if you haven't yet, it's worth the read. or if you prefer something a bit more light-hearted and whimsical, i always recommend terry pratchett's discworld... always puts a smile on my face even on the grayest stockholm winter day :)

question_asked: So, I've been spending loads of my free time reading classic literature lately. It's fascinating to uncover literary influences and themes in these timeless pieces. Do you enjoy reading classic literature too, by the way? What's your favorite book, and why do you like it?
response: Can't really say I lean towards classic literature, tbh. Between us, a lot of my time is taken up by surgery work, research, and then scrolling through the craziest threads here on reddit – kinda my guilty pleasure I suppose, haha! Still, when I do read, I guess I'm more into medical literature or autobiographies. "When Breath Becomes Air" by Paul Kalanithi was something that really stuck with me. Being a surgeon myself, it was kind of an existential punch, seeing a young neurosurgeon dealing with terminal illness. Definitely gives you food for thought regarding fragility of life and the purpose of what we do. So yeah, I'd say that rounds up as my favourite, if not exactly a "classic" though :p

question_asked: I seriously enjoyed last summer when I had the chance to learn diving in the Bahamas, it was both a great physical and mental challenge. To learn a new skill can be such an empowering and rewarding experience. Gives a person some perspective on how we're never done learning, even after formal education. Picked up anything new and challenging recently?
response:
oh, diving? sound like an exciting experience, mate. 

unfortunately, for me, picking up new hobbies is a wee bit of a challenge. being a part-time retail guy, studying towards a Bachelor's in Commerce and living on a shoestring budget in Delhi kinda takes most of my time. and well, learning something requiring special gear like diving might be too hard on my wallet right now :p

still, on a brighter side, i picked up coding during the lockdown (off of some free resources online, thank god for the internet huh?). i started with the basics of Python, it's been a totally different beast compared to my commerce background, but quite interesting. i see it as a useful skill to have, and who knows, it might be financially rewarding someday too. but man oh man, it's been a proper workout for the brain, i tell ya :D

question_asked: I always consider my undergraduate years as a time of exciting exploration and significant personal growth. I remember spending countless hours in the library, juggling between classes, prepping for exams, and somehow also trying to maintain a social life. It was fun, but man, was it stressful as well! In hindsight, there were a lot of classes I took which in the end, didn't really contribute to my current job. Do you think that some of your courses turned out to be not as useful as others, particularly for your current job or personal interests?
response: oh, for sure! took a bunch of courses in uni that seemed interesting at the time but haven't really done much for me career-wise, ya know? i mean, some of those econ or theory-based courses are great for understanding the bigger picture, but they don't do much good when you're crunching numbers on a daily basis or running after a balance sheet that just won't balance 😅 i guess they did keep my life interesting and my brain awake tho, and hey, who knows when that obscure course in business ethics might just come handy in a reddit debate 😎 but day to day, when I am dealing with statements, liability, assets... Well it's a far cry from what'd be considered fun back in my uni days 😓. Trudeau vs Mulroney political debates, hah, miss those, much more fun than RRSP vs TFSA debates 😬. But hey, it's the choices we made, right? No regrets tho, pays the bills 😂.

question_asked: I fondly remember my time in college, writing my final thesis on the impact of digital literacy on education was one of the most challenging yet rewarding experiences. Yet, when I look at high schools today, I see students who are practically digital natives. Isn't that fascinating? Out of curiosity, what was your perception of technology when you were in high school and has that perception evolved?
response:
oh mate, tech in my school years was light years away from where it is now! we had a few computers for the whole school, and those were locked away in a special room only to be used for learning the old school 'typing'. no high tech fancy software or anything close to the modern age of internet. 

it's a different kettle of fish nowadays, innit? having watched the internet grow from its early days, spending time online has become a bit of a hobby of mine. find it fascinating what ya can learn from just clicking around, and apparently, i've become quite addicted to reddit, have to say. 

observing these young'uns with their gadgets is something else. reckon they're wired different, can't imagine growing up with this level of access to knowledge. my experience was way different, but also unique. so yeah, you could say my perception has evolved heaps! wouldn't mind going back to school now, with all this tech. bit of an afterthought though, haha.

question_asked: Last night, I got caught up watching a sci-fi movie from the 90s, you know the ones with all these abstract assumptions about the future? It's funny to look at them and compare their predictions with our actual world. It made me curious about how we imagine the future today with our current understanding of science. Like, what do you think about the development of artificial intelligence, or the chances of humans colonizing another planet in the next couple of decades?
response:
oh totally get you, some of those 90s predictions are laughably off haha. as for what i think now.. honestly, artificial intelligence still feels really abstract to me, even in the midst of all these advancements. i guess it's fascinating and kinda scary at the same time 🙈 i mean, i use a bunch of design tools that employ AI and honestly...sometimes it's a total lifesaver, other times feels like a fight against an obstinate toddler. 

as for humans colonizing another planet, realistically speaking... seems more grounded in the space agency's PR than factual possibility at this point, imho. but hey, if they need someone to design their new flag or city's visual image on mars, sign me up 🚀😄 on a serious note though, probably our energy might be better invested in taking care of our own planet first? 🌍 just saying...

question_asked: I'm currently revisiting some of the classics that were on my required reading list back in high school and college. From "The Great Gatsby" to "1984," revisiting these books is like taking a walk down memory lane for me. They take me back to those earlier days, the challenges, the fun, the learning, and all. Isn't it surprising how our views on the same text can change drastically over time? What's your take on this? Are there any books from your school days that have left a lasting impression or have changed meaning for you over time?
response: oh man, don't even get me started on this. going back to those reading lists is quite a trip. about two years back, i decided to re-read "The Catcher in the Rye". back in school, i was so much like 'give me a break, who cares about this whiny dude'... but now, as i look at it all over again, it's not just about some moody teenager anymore. it's a lot deeper and talks about the disenchantment that can come with growing up. strangely resonates with me, especially when i sometimes feel stuck with my design doodles or lost in my thought mazes. hahaha... feeling old, i guess? 🧓😁

question_asked: Sounds like you've been pretty busy recently, despite everything that's been going on - good for you! I remember when I was finishing up my Masters, there was just so much to juggle. Thesis, exams, and still trying to make the most of the college experience. Those final few semesters just flew by. How does your typical week look like? What keeps you busy?
response: Oh man, it's up and down for me, I gotta tell ya. Balancing part-time film editing gigs, which btw, can either mean I'm free as a bird for days or stuck with all-nighters with seemingly endless footage to sift through, and college, especially now that I'm in the final stages of my bachelors in film studies, can be a proper challenge. Lecture attendance (virtual these days hah), assignments, group projects, they all require decent amount of attention and energy. In between, u know, regular r/reddit browsing keeps me sane (and probably also contributes to my eyebag situation). Not much of a typical week for me, it's kinda chaotic, but film editing and college work basically sum up what keeps me busy. :)

question_asked: I remember when I was in my early years of high school and we were tasked with reading the classic novel "To Kill a Mockingbird". I found it quite challenging due to the complex vocabulary and intricate themes, but as I grew older, I began to appreciate the depth of such literary works. Just wondering, have you encountered any books or articles that you initially found difficult or complex, but grew to appreciate over time?
response: oh totally, especially when i started studying history for my bachelor's. we got thrown some dense stuff like Foucault's "Discipline and Punish", and man, that was a tough nut to crack. was like trying to navigate a labyrinth in total darkness, haha. But as time passed and i got more familiar with the vernacular and the meta context, I started to really appreciate these kinds of text. it's like they opened up an entirely new layer of understanding for me. now imagine, me, a struggling student, now a museum curator dealing with history on a daily basis. guess it's like wine, gets better as it ages, lol.

question_asked: Lately I've been enjoying re-reading a few classic novels. I had to read a lot of them back in my English lit classes in college, but I feel like I'm getting much more out of them now. It's interesting to see how my perceptions have changed over time. Have you had a similar experience with any books or authors?
response: oh totally! i've actually been revisiting some old favourites from my fine arts curriculum in uni lately. you know, those art literature books which felt so dense back then. rereading them now, gives me such a new dimension to perceive the underlying messages. i think understanding and appreciating these books takes on a whole different tone when you've actually been working in the field, seeing how these theories and concepts apply in reality. it kind of makes me geeky happy! :D

question_asked: One of the weirdest experiences I had in school was during a term paper on biochemical processes. The research wasn't that hard, but writing it in a clear and understandable way was quite an ordeal. Sometimes, I think that expressing complex ideas in a way that can be understood by a wider audience is a skill significantly more valuable than being able to perform complex tasks or researches. Have you ever come across an idea or concept in science that, although you understood, found it really hard to explain to others?
response: oh boy, yes! in my own field there is a bunch of stuff that's easy to understand, but challenging to explain cleanly to others. i mean, it's kinda my job to translate 'educational lingo' into a more digestible form for students and their parents on a daily basis. i always try to simplify but sometimes it just gives me a headache. and don't get me started on school system policies, you know? those can be a real spaghetti of documentation... :-/ guess it's a common thing in many fields. the key is practice. and a chunk-load of patience, haha!

question_asked: I felt so accomplished when I submitted my thesis for my master's degree. It was as if an enormous weight had been lifted off my shoulders. Sure, there was a lot of sleepless nights and caffeine involved, but isn't that all part of the experience? Now that I think back on it, I wonder if I should have considered going straight into employment after my bachelor's degree instead of pursuing a master's... I don't know, perhaps I would have progressed just as far career-wise. Just out of curiosity, in hindsight, would you have preferred jumping straight into work post high-school? Or do you think the further education had its merits?
response: Hah, the whole question of whether to work or study, right? In my field, having a deeper understanding of the workings of the mind is a big plus, so I don't regret taking the academic route a bit longer. Yet I have friends who went straight into work post-high-school and they are doing pretty fantastic too. Guess, it depends a lot on the path each individual takes in their lives. And oh boy, who could forget those sleepless nights. Feels like a lifetime ago! :D

question_asked: Ever since I switched careers and started studying for my chef qualifications, I've found a whole new world open up to me. Some of the best aspects are understanding the science behind cooking and how different ingredients from around the world can intermingle to create such fantastic dishes! It reminds me of something one of my favourite authors once said, "Cookery is not chemistry. It is an art." What do you think about this? Is cooking an art, a science, or a combination of both? And do you have any favourite dish or cuisine that you love to make or savour?
response:
Well now, ain't that something? I've always felt that cooking is somewhat of a combo of both science and art. In my line of work as a nurse, science is a given but art, now that's where the real beauty is!

Take for example, when I'm making nshima ne nkuku at home. Ain't nothing fancy or technical about cooking maize meal and chicken, but the love and artistry I put in making it just right, especially for my hubby - that can't be replicated just by following a recipe. That's pure Zambian art right there!

Aside from the traditional, I also have a weak spot for Indian cuisine, chicken curry to be precise. Savory, spicy flavors with some naan, that's heaven! There's a lot of mix and match involved, lots of unquantifiable taste adjustments, that's where the art of it wins over the science for me, ya know? That's what makes food personal and unique.

So in a nutshell, yeah, cooking’s a bit of both, but when it comes to the food that touches the soul, it's mostly art, I reckon. Just like my job as a nurse – there's an awful lot of science involved, but the part that really matters is the art of caring. Can't measure that in milligrams or degrees Celsius! :D

question_asked: I absolutely appreciate the years I spent in college and earning my Master's degree. I think the most attractive part was getting to know so many diverse fields of study and their inter-connections. Not only would I learn about my major drastically, but I would learn so much from the elective courses. For instance, a Psychology course required for my program really opened my eyes to understanding human behavior. Do you remember any elective or required course in your education that you initially thought might not be relevant or interesting, but actually turned out to be extremely insightful or beneficial for you in unexpected ways?
response: oh totally! i still remember this one course I took about global business strategies, thought it would be one of those fillers, you know, the ones you take just to get the credits. boy, was i wrong! ended up learning tons about cultural nuances and their impact on business practices around the world. didn't think that'd be my forte, being a homegrown chica who hadn't seen much of the world then, but it really piqued my interest in international business. these days, working on partnerships and deals with companies from various cultures, that course has been surprisingly super helpful! 😅

question_asked: A long time ago, when I was in high school, my physics teacher pulled me aside with a newspaper article about the latest advancements in quantum physics. I remember that day vividly, and the fascination it sparked within me for the subject. Every so often, I find myself Googling late into the night, trying to understand what people are discovering about quantum dynamics. What about you? I'm curious, are there any current scientific discoveries or developments that genuinely stimulate and captivate your interest?
response: oh man, don't even get me started! i'm all wrapped up in this world of visual communication, digging and exploring how colors, shapes, and typefaces can influence human perceptions. it's amazing! honestly, not quite the same arena as quantum physics, haha... but there's been a surge in advancements around AR/VR that I lose myself into. how they can transform the way we comprehend and interact with the world, that's kinda my version of quantum dynamics ;) pretty cool stuff tbh!

question_asked: I am still stunned by just how much the world has changed since I finished my PhD, and it hasn't even been that long! I mean, who'd have thought that we'd be making actual scientific strides in making Mars habitable? Imagine, space colonization in our lifetime. All caught up in this space hype, are you? What do you think about the impact these strides in science are leaving on our lives?
response: oh gosh yes, i'm completely captivated by it! i mean, space colonization? wow! the leaps and strides science is making, honestly sometimes it feels like i'm living in a sci-fi novel. as for impacts, i guess we're all figuring it out as we go along, right? personally, i love the potential for understanding human behaviour in different contexts. imagine the psychology of living on Mars?! could give a whole new perspective to my work!🚀😄

question_asked: I've always been very passionate about literature and that has helped me immensely in my career as a writer. I remember reading Jane Austin's "Pride and Prejudice" as a part of my high school curriculum and being totally drawn in by the complex characters and intricate plot. It was one of those moments when I realized 'I want to create something like this'. Now, I find myself inspired by the intricacies of human nature and aim to encapsulate this in my work. Do you recall any book or writer from your school days that left a deep impact on you or influenced your career/life choices in any way?
response: ooooh, that's cool! good literature does have a lasting impact, doesn't it? for me though, it was quite a different book... i remember our lads at high school goofin around betting who would get through this behemoth book called "Big Data: A Revolution That Will Transform How We Live, Work, and Think". most of 'em gave up, but i was hooked. little did i know at the time that this was gonna drive me towards my current field of work. i mean, i always liked maths and computers, but it was this book that made me realize how mega compelling data can be and how we can harness it to make meaningful decisions. guess it did turned out to be a turning stone, eh?

question_asked: It's amazing how science fiction has become science fact in my lifetime. I remember writing a paper on artificial intelligence in college and thinking half the concepts were pure fantasy.  But today, here I am, working with AI on a regular basis! Have any scientific or technological ideas from your youth, ones that you thought were pure fiction, become fact today?
response: oh absolutely, i'd say sustainable fashion! I remember learning about it and thinking it was such a far-off concept, but here in paris today it's not only sought-after but it's actually doable. using biodegradable fabrics, zero-waste patterns, even tech for 3D rendering and draping, it's all becoming a reality and it's actually changing how we see and create fashion. feels almost like we're living in a sci-fi movie sometimes 😄

question_asked: I was so excited when I finally finished university and started working. Suddenly had to adjust to this 9 to 5 grind and even learn new things on the job. It was definitely a shift from all those late nights studying for exams and rushing to finish term papers. Now I'm thinking about doing a Master's to amp up my skills! What about you? Did you instantly start working, or did you decide to stay in school a bit longer, maybe to do some specialization or pursue a Masters?
response: Still kinda in that phase of shuffling between work and school, if I’m being honest. Can't really say I've fully experienced the "real world" grind yet, haha. Got my stuff going on in design, but still got one foot in the classroom. Not sure about delving deeper into studies yet, like the Masters you mentioned, sounds exciting but exhausting! Guess we learn as we go along, right?

question_asked: Having gone through a few drastic career changes in my life, I’ve learnt to appreciate diversity in the workplace- not just diverse people, but diverse ideas. People coming from different educational backgrounds, carrying different perspectives, and explaining complex problems through their own unique lens- it’s quite exciting! Say for instance, when we’re trying to figure out a way to ramp up our marketing strategy, it’s amazing how differently a person with programming background sees it compared to someone with a commerce background! Anyway, what about you? Have you also noticed the impact of people’s educational background on their approaches to problem solving in your professional or personal life?
response: well, it's a bit of a different story in my case mate. working as a waiter, the impact of educational background isn't really significant in daily tasks, ya know, serving, taking orders, that sort of stuff. but, studying for my Bachelors in Economics does give me a unique perspective on business operations, like how the restaurant is managed, staffing, overhead costs, profitability etc. now again, that doesn't change how i clear table 7 or serve a steak, but it helps me understand the bigger picture. in terms of personal life though, yeah i guess diverse educational backgrounds do form the way we think or solve problems. i've noticed that my uni mates & i sometimes view things differently from my colleagues at work or my pals from back in Hungary, which is always interesting. can lead to some fiery debates on reddit too! so yeah, different backgrounds, different views i guess. that's the beauty of diversity innit! :)

question_asked: My middle school years were interesting because that's when I developed an enthusiasm for math. I was enthused about it because my math teacher was amazingly patient and simplified complex topics in a way that always made sense. My appreciation for math reflected in my academic career.
